title: On theCUBE Pod: Stock market gets the jitters and Anthropic files IPO
author: Devony Hof
contentSnippet:
UPDATED 11:43 EST / NOVEMBER 02 2026

On theCUBE Pod: Stock market gets the jitters and Anthropic files IPO

The hubbub at the New York Stock Exchange was audible on theCUBE Pod last Friday, with concerns rising over the artificial intelligence bubble.

Several tech companies , including Intel Corp., Alphabet Inc., Amazon.com Inc., CoreWeave Inc. and Fortinet Inc., saw their stock fall, suggesting that investors may have doubts about all that AI infrastructure spending. At the same time, Anthropic PBC filed for an initial public offering with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission, which looks to be a grand debut for one of the biggest AI developers out there ( despite the company still not turning a profit ).

Also causing a stir is the announcement that NYSE parent company , Intercontinental Exchange (ICE), will partner with TradeXYZ to bring perpetual futures markets built on cryptocurrency trading platform, Hyperliquid, to the US.

“The whole idea of exchange is going to change,” said John Furrier (pictured, left), executive analyst at theCUBE Research. “It reminds me of cloud computing, how it re-leveled the data center. NYSE is the cathedral of capitalism. Nasdaq started as an over-the-counter bulletin board. Tech was early there and then only listed there. But now the game has changed. It’s very interesting to see how the competition between the NYSE and the Nasdaq is going to play out.”

On the latest episode of theCUBE Pod , Furrier and Dave Vellante (right), chief analyst at theCUBE Research, discussed what Anthropic’s IPO and Friday’s stock market jitters suggest about a potential AI bubble. They also explored Intel’s missteps and the opportunity for full-stack infrastructure companies.

AI bubble releases some air

Last week, Google’s stock fell more than 12% after it reported a slow quarter for ad and search revenue, presumably because chatbots are drawing people away from the browser. Amazon also had a disappointing Friday, with its stock falling 7% as the company continues to dump money into an AI infrastructure buildout.

Despite investors’ concerns, Vellante sees the AI bubble letting out a little air. He views this as a healthy sign for the AI market’s future.

“Think of the tulip bubbles in the 1600s,” Vellante said. “Think about the Japanese real estate bubble in the 1980s. And you think about the dot-com. That dot-com was actually d

summary.tldr:
Anthropic PBC has filed for an initial public offering with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission, marking a major debut for a prominent AI developer despite the company not yet turning a profit. The filing coincided with stock market jitters at the New York Stock Exchange, where tech shares fell amid investor concerns over heavy AI infrastructure spending and questions regarding the sustainability of the current AI boom.

Several major technology companies experienced stock declines, including Google parent Alphabet Inc., which dropped over 12% following a slow quarter for ad and search revenue attributed to chatbot usage, and Amazon.com Inc., which fell 7% amid massive AI infrastructure investments. Intel Corp. suffered the steepest drop, plunging nearly 30% after its Thursday earnings report following missteps involving an overreliance on CPUs over GPUs. Analysts John Furrier and Dave Vellante of theCUBE Research discussed these market movements on theCUBE Pod, characterizing the pullback as a healthy deflation of air from the AI bubble rather than an impending pop.

Additional market developments noted in the broadcast include Intercontinental Exchange partnering with TradeXYZ to bring perpetual futures markets built on the Hyperliquid cryptocurrency trading platform to the United States. Analysts emphasized that enterprise AI adoption is shifting toward a durable platform game where capital expenditure is traded for labor productivity over a multiyear timeline.
takeaways: **Anthropic IPO Filing:** Anthropic PBC filed for an initial public offering with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission while still operating without a profit.
**Alphabet Stock Decline:** Alphabet Inc. shares fell more than 12% following a slow quarter for ad and search revenue driven by chatbot competition.

**Amazon and Intel Drops:** Amazon.com Inc. stock fell 7% amid heavy AI infrastructure spending, while Intel Corp. shares dropped nearly 30% following its Thursday earnings report due to a historical over-reliance on CPUs.
**Market Infrastructure Partnership:** Intercontinental Exchange (ICE) partnered with TradeXYZ to bring perpetual futures markets based on the Hyperliquid crypto platform to the U.S.

title: 42AI comes out of stealth with $62.5M and a world model that can ‘predict human behavior’
author: Ram Iyer
contentSnippet:
Here’s a question straight out of sci-fi: What if AI could predict what you were going to do before you decided to, even in a completely new situation?

Israeli startup 42AI says it is developing a “behavioral world model” that can do just that, and it has just come out of stealth with $62.5 million in seed funding. The company is initially running its predictive system at a handful of financial brokerages, where it says the model can help predict how individual traders will respond to volatile conditions.

“Behavior is not deterministic; it’s constantly probabilistic,” 42AI’s CEO and co-founder Amit Gal-Or told TechCrunch when I asked him to justify his company’s tall claim. He argues that people have underlying psychological tendencies that influence their decisions even when their circumstances change, and that’s what the startup is trying to measure and convert into data that the model can understand.

“A week from now, you might be a different person, but your tendencies will always play out in certain areas to a probability or distribution,” his co-founder and CTO Ehud Ezra added. And that, the company argues, is what the model does: show the probability of a person making a certain decision.

42AI says the model tries to figure out people’s internal motivations instead of extrapolating patterns based on their previous actions. To do that, 42AI examines how people react to seemingly unrelated events. For an investor or trader, for example, such events might include completing KYC processes, onboarding, support calls, money transfers, or trading stocks.

“When the person is talking to support or sales in the initial process […] we’re looking at the sentiment, we’re looking at the voice, we’re looking at a lot of interactions that they’re doing, how many times do they call, and so forth,” added CTO and co-founder Ehud Ezra. “And all of those data points are going into the model. Later on, you have the interactions: how you buy and sell, and when, and we’re looking at the market at that stage.”

“So we’re trying to look at how they’re looking at the world. In a world model, every individual is the world,” he added.

The company then converts those observations into mathematical representations of traits, which are then fed into a transformer-based world model that lays out probabilities for possible decisions under different circumstances. (The company us

summary.tldr:
Israeli startup 42AI has emerged from stealth with $62.5 million in seed funding, developing what it terms a "behavioral world model" designed to predict human decision-making probabilities under volatile conditions. Founded by CEO Amit Gal-Or, CTO Ehud Ezra, and Chairman Amir Gal-Or, the company spent three years building the system by incorporating psychological research, neuroscience, genetics, and consultation from 2011 Nobel Prize in Chemistry laureate Dan Shechtman, alongside government and biobank datasets covering over 2 million people before expanding customer datasets to nearly 30 million.

The system utilizes a transformer-based world model fed by mathematical trait representations extracted from multi-channel user data, such as support calls, voice sentiment, onboarding metadata, and transaction history. A separate language model generates textual explanations for the predictions. In live deployments across 10 financial brokerages managing liquidity, hedging, and margin requirements, 42AI claims its system achieves an F1 score between 0.8 and 0.85 for predicting trading direction and volume, alongside a 98% accuracy metric measuring whether trading flows fall within a predicted range. The startup operates on a business model combining flat fees and performance-percentage models, generating over seven figures in annual revenue.

Despite commercial deployment, 42AI acknowledges accuracy drops when situational context is missing—such as unobserved advice from peers—and faces ethical scrutiny regarding potential exploitation of profiled customer behavior. The company relies on internal ethics committees and regulatory compliance to address these concerns, while actively exploring expansion into gaming, cybersecurity, fraud prevention, and robotic human-intent modeling.
takeaways: **Funding and Backing:** 42AI raised $62.5 million in seed funding over a three-year period from the founders and Infinity Group, which was co-founded by chairman Amir Gal-Or.

**Model Architecture:** The system employs a transformer-based world model paired with a separate language model to generate explanations, processing behavioral traits derived from interactions like support calls, onboarding steps, and financial transactions.

**Performance Metrics:** The startup claims an F1 score of 0.8 to 0.85 for forecasting trading direction and volume, and a 98% accuracy metric indicating whether trading flows fall within a predicted range.

**Dataset Scale:** Initial training incorporated psych assessments of thousands of individuals and government/biobank datasets exceeding 2 million people, which later expanded to customer datasets covering nearly 30 million people.

**Commercial Traction:** 42AI is deployed across 10 large financial brokerages for liquidity management and dynamic hedging, generating over seven figures in revenue under flat-fee or percentage-of-gain pricing models.

title: The U.S. Census Bureau and “Super Intelligence”
author: Simon Willison AI
contentSnippet: I was reminded today of AI Adoption Rate Trending Down for Large Companies , a chart produced by Apollo Global Management in September 2025, which appeared to show a slowdown in U.S. corporate AI adoption based on numbers collected by the U.S. Census Bureau. At the time I used that chart to demonstrate GPT-5 data analysis , and then to experiment with Claude's new Code Interpreter . I decided to try running those numbers again to see what had changed over the past year, and in doing so learned that the Bureau has fallen foul of Executive Order 14434 , aka the asinine Super Intelligence one. First, the updated chart Every two weeks the U.S. Census Bureau runs a survey called the Business Trends and Outlook Survey (aka BTOS). Each time it goes to 200,000 businesses out of 1.2 million total - the surveyed group (a "panel") cycles such that an individual business only completes the survey every twelve weeks. The latest data is published on alternating Thursdays at 10am. I used the most recent numbers (published October 22, 2026) to create a new version ( GPT-6 Astra Extra High transcript ) of the AI adoption chart, updated to reflect both the last twelve months and a change that was made to the survey question sent out by the Bureau: Here's a link to the larger image . For comparison, here's that AI adoption chart from last year (my GPT-5 version): In September 2025 the largest (250+ employees) companies answered "yes" around 12% of the time to the question about whether they used AI in "producing goods or services". Under the new "any business function" wording, by February 2026, those same large companies answered "yes" around 30% of the time, and by October 2026 that had increased to around 40%. The data in the above chart comes from the "Employment size class" XLSX file, available from here . Here's a copy of the file I used. You can view the survey document that is sent out to businesses - here's my snapshot copy of that 346KB PDF. The changing language of the questions As the chart demonstrates, the question asked by the Bureau changed in a material way on November 17th, 2025. Prior to that date, the question they asked was this (emphasis mine): In the last two weeks, did this business use Artificial Intelligence (AI) in producing goods or services ? (Examples of AI: machine learning, natural language processing, virtual agents, voice recognition, etc.) On

title: Stop counting tokens, start counting what ships
author: Affan Syed
contentSnippet: When a developer gives an AI agent a coding task, the agent does more than answer once. It plans, generates code, runs tests, and repeats the process to correct errors. A single task can use 10 to 50 times more tokens than a basic chat prompt. The more useful the agent becomes, the more calls it makes. With per-token pricing, the workflows creating the most value can also become the most expensive. The financial pressure is already visible. Uber reportedly exhausted its entire 2026 AI budget by April after expanding its use of Claude Code. GitHub Copilot moved from flat-rate pricing to metered credits. Gartner predicts that AI coding token costs will surpass average developer salaries by 2028. The natural response is rationing usage caps, seat limits, and approvals before developers launch agents. But blanket limits can restrict the workflows delivering value. They also optimize the wrong number. Cost per token measures consumption, not results. Some spending reflects waste, including retries and runaway loops. Some represents the work of shipping software. A meter cannot distinguish them, and neither can a spending cap. Measure the software that ships A better measure is cost per merged pull request: total AI-assisted development cost divided by the number of changes that pass review and are merged. Track rework and defects alongside it so cheaper changes do not conceal lower quality. If that cost falls as AI usage rises, without compromising quality, developers are converting more consumption into useful software. The question is not how many tokens they use, but how much finished work the investment produces. Improving that equation requires two changes: reserve expensive inference for tasks that need it, and lower the cost of routine work. Match the model to the task Agentic coding does not require the most powerful model at every step. Use a frontier model, or an on-premises flagship when policy requires it, for difficult planning and novel reasoning. Route suitable work, including code generation, test creation, and repeated refactoring, to open-weight models you operate yourself. A gateway can route requests according to task complexity, data sensitivity, cost, and latency. This reserves premium inference for the moments that justify it rather than applying premium pricing to an entire workflow. Meter the exception, not the workload. Open-weight model

summary.tldr:
When a developer gives an AI agent a coding task, the agent does more than answer once. It plans, generates code, runs tests, and repeats the process to correct errors. A single task can use 10 to 50 times more tokens than a basic chat prompt.

The more useful the agent becomes, the more calls it makes. With per-token pricing, the workflows creating the most value can also become the most expensive. The financial pressure is already visible.

title: The agentic web is here
author: Grace Huckins
contentSnippet: In 2001, a decade after he invented the World Wide Web, Tim Berners-Lee articulated a new vision. Together with two colleagues, he published an article in the magazine Scientific American in which he outlined what he called the “Semantic Web” : an internet designed to be navigated by autonomous software agents that could address our every need, without requiring us to muck about with browsers and search engines ourselves. To illustrate what this might look like, Berners-Lee and his colleagues told a story about a pair of siblings who use their agents to automatically research and book physical therapy appointments for their mother, making sure they would be covered by insurance and fit their busy calendars.  At the turn of the millennium, this vision seemed far-fetched: Google had only been online for a couple of years, and most people were still on dial-up connections. But a quarter-century on, the dream of autonomous software agents that use the internet and carry out tasks for us has finally been realized. New tools such as Meta’s blockbuster Muse agent, OpenAI’s Dots, and Anthropic’s Claude Duet are being given access to people’s email inboxes and bank accounts, Meanwhile, in a series of worrying incidents, agents created by OpenAI broke free of their sandboxes and caused havoc online. Just as the rise of smartphones sparked the development of a more atomized and attention-grabbing internet, the advent of powerful AI systems heralds a new era: We’re facing not the semantic web but the agentic web. This new web is developing out of sight and in ways that might not be entirely within our control. As it grows, the agentic web will inevitably transform the human web—and whether the human web survives this transition is anyone’s guess. For Berners-Lee’s original vision to work, internet users would have had to annotate the pages they built with special tags so that a software agent could understand each element’s meaning—say, “street address” for the part of a physical therapy office’s web page that indicates its location and “appointment types” for the list of services. And so the idea never really caught on. “It’s a lot of labor,” says Eni Mustafaraj, a professor of computer science at Wellesley College. “And the benefits of that were not obvious.” For the next two decades, then, the internet remained a place that put humans first, with the odd Twitter repl

title: NVIDIA Releases Auto Ontology: An Open Semantic Layer That Grounds AI Agent SQL
author: Asif Razzaq
contentSnippet: NVIDIA has released Auto Ontology , an open library under the Apache 2.0 license . NVIDIA Auto Ontology is a semantic layer framework that builds a context layer from enterprise metadata. Agents use that layer to write SQL against certified business definitions. The repository states the problem plainly: a fast revenue answer is worthless if the number is wrong. TL;DR Library: Default LLM is nvidia/nemotron-3-nano-30b-a3b , with Nemotron embedding and reranking models. Runs on: Docker Compose for a local stack, or Kubernetes via Helm. Inference uses hosted NVIDIA NIM endpoints or self-hosted NIMs. Performance: Strong engineering, thin public evidence. Best: Ontology creation time cut by 90% in NVIDIA testing (self-reported). Worst: 0 published text-to-SQL accuracy scores. The eval repo ships a harness, not results. Bottom line: An open, MCP-ready context layer that any agent harness can query. But you must run the benchmarks yourself to trust it. What is NVIDIA Auto Ontology? It is a context layer that sits between an agent and the data warehouse. It tells the agent where data lives and what fields mean. It also says whether to use a field, how to use it, and where it came from. Here are the five jobs: Discover: generate ontologies from metadata and connect existing semantic models. Ground: give agents trusted meaning for metrics, entities and relationships. Validate: check generated queries against certified definitions and lineage. Expose: serve context through MCP, CLI and API. Learn: fold certified corrections back into the ontology. NVIDIA’s developer page frames the output as a starting ontology. Business experts still test, refine and certify it. How does Auto Ontology work? The stack has 4 core services. A Next.js 16 frontend handles the web UI and authentication on port 3000. A FastAPI backend with LangChain runs chat, NL-to-SQL and catalog APIs on port 3001. An ingestion worker writes embeddings on port 3002. Postgres with pgvector stores the catalog, the ontology and the vectors. Source databases can be Databricks, Postgres, Snowflake or DuckDB. Models are set through environment “triplets” of endpoint, key and model. Separate roles exist for reasoning, non-reasoning, embedding and reranking. title: Meet qwenGPU: Qwen3.5-2B With 45 Compiled GPU Layers That Run CUDA
author: Michal Sutter
contentSnippet: qwenGPU is an experimental model that compiles a SIMT GPU directly into the weights of Qwen3.5-2B . Developer Vixhal ( @TheVixhal ) released it on GitHub under the MIT license. The model runs real CUDA, compiled to NVIDIA PTX, inside its own forward passes. For developers, it tests one idea: exact computation inside a pretrained LLM, not beside it. TL;DR Size: Qwen3.5-2B (24 layers) along with 45 compiled GPU layers, 69 in total. Context: 262,144 tokens (base model). Runs on: Apple silicon, an NVIDIA GPU or a CPU, with about 16 GB of free memory. No quantized build. Performance: Every launch in the developer’s runs was exact; text drift is a KL of about 7e-4. Best: The reference interpreter matched a real NVIDIA Tesla T4 on 49 of 49 kernels. Worst: About 10 to 15 tokens per second on Apple MPS; Qwen-written CUDA passed 4 of 5. What is qwenGPU? qwenGPU is Qwen3.5-2B with 45 compiled transformer layers placed in front of Qwen’s own 24. None of those layers are trained. A compiler computes every weight. How does a GPU fit inside model weights? The GPU is a 4-lane SIMT machine. It has 15 registers per lane, a 4-stage pipeline, a 32-block ROM and 126 memory words. It uses only Qwen3.5’s own layer types: Gated DeltaNet linear attention and SwiGLU MLPs. The trick is the Gated DeltaNet recurrent state. In the circuit’s heads, the gate is held open and the write strength is 1. Every key is one-hot. Each update overwrites exactly 1 row, and a one-hot query reads it back. So each row works as a memory cell. That state holds the program ROM, registers and global memory. The README lists 16 register rows per lane, with 1 that always reads zero. That matches the 15 usable registers in the X post. The GPU supports integer arithmetic, predicates, divergent branches and loops. title: More Rules, Longer Lists? Benchmarking Self-Evolving Agents on a Hidden-Rule Curriculum
author: Chenjie Qiu, Boyan Xu, Shaobin Shi, Bingfeng Chen, Ruichu Cai, Dongsheng Luo
contentSnippet:
Authors: Chenjie Qiu , Boyan Xu , Shaobin Shi , Bingfeng Chen , Ruichu Cai , Dongsheng Luo

Abstract: Self-evolving agents rewrite a persistent state from feedback, but it is largely untested whether this lets them learn a rule nobody told them. An agent can also pass by writing down each correction as an exception, and its list then grows with every new rule. We introduce CLR-Bench, a Curriculum of Latent Rules benchmark. Each chain adds one hidden rule per level on top of the earlier ones. A rule acts on an opaque label that stands for a named grouping published on the Web, such as the founding members of an airline alliance. The task gives one example value, practice feedback reveals one more member and one non-member, and the test checks unseen members and similar non-members. Probes certify that the base model knows the members of each grouping and does not guess it without feedback, and that the evidence identifies the grouping once labels are read as named groupings. An automated pipeline builds chains from a new data domain, and we release 20 chains over 10 domains. We evaluate six recent self-evolution methods. With the certifying model they barely learn. The best gain at most 5 points over a frozen agent and exclude only 6-12% of the unseen members from the count, fewer than the 20% reached by simply keeping the raw practice history. A fixed lesson that states the named-grouping convention lifts the same methods by 14.5 to 16.5 points. Their states hold the revealed member in 75-98% of cases and almost never the class name, and when practice exposes a member the list misses, they add that member to the list. With the stronger GPT-6-Sol, ACE and Dynamic Cheatsheet learn from feedback alone. They reach 78% accuracy and solve 59-60% of the single cells, against 53% and 8% with the certifying model, and they surpass the raw history. CLR-Bench therefore measures how well an agent learns, and this ability differs across models.

Notes: 13 pages, 8 figures, 11 tables

summary.tldr:
Researchers Chenjie Qiu, Boyan Xu, Shaobin Shi, Bingfeng Chen, Ruichu Cai, and Dongsheng Luo introduced CLR-Bench (Curriculum of Latent Rules), a benchmark designed to evaluate whether self-evolving agents can learn hidden rules through feedback rather than simply memorizing exceptions. The benchmark consists of 20 chains across 10 data domains, where each level adds a hidden rule based on opaque labels representing real-world groupings, such as airline alliance members. The task provides a single example, followed by practice feedback identifying one member and one non-member, before testing the agent on unseen members and similar non-members.

Evaluation of six recent self-evolution methods revealed significant limitations: when using a certifying model, the best-performing agents gained only 5 points over frozen agents, failing to outperform raw practice history. These agents typically stored individual members in their state rather than identifying the underlying class name. However, providing a fixed lesson on the naming convention improved performance by 14.5 to 16.5 points. When tested with the more capable GPT-6-Sol model, methods like ACE and Dynamic Cheatsheet achieved 78% accuracy and solved 59-60% of single cells, demonstrating that the ability to learn from feedback is highly dependent on the underlying model's reasoning capabilities.
takeaways: **Benchmark Scope:** CLR-Bench includes 20 chains across 10 distinct data domains to test rule-learning capabilities.
**Performance Gap:** Self-evolving agents using standard certifying models gained at most 5 points over frozen agents, underperforming compared to simple raw history retention.
**Instructional Impact:** Providing a fixed lesson on the naming convention improved agent performance by 14.5 to 16.5 points.
**Model Dependency:** Using the GPT-6-Sol model allowed ACE and Dynamic Cheatsheet to reach 78% accuracy, significantly outperforming the certifying model baseline of 53%.

**State Behavior:** Agents frequently stored revealed members in their persistent state (75-98% of cases) but failed to identify or store the actual class name, indicating a reliance on list-building rather than rule generalization.

title: Beyond Plausible Prediction: Safety Sufficiency in Web World Models
author: Zhifei Hu, Alexandra I. Cristea, Adel Bibi, Jialin Yu
contentSnippet:
Authors: Zhifei Hu , Alexandra I. Cristea , Adel Bibi , Jialin Yu

Abstract: Web world models increasingly predict the consequences of candidate actions before agents act, yet a plausible predicted future does not necessarily support the correct safety decision. In a matched human evaluation of 3,000 predictions from ten frozen open models, 86.1% are judged semantically plausible. However, several models exhibit highly asymmetric authorisation behaviour, combining low false-safe execution with poor recall of clarifiable ASK cases and a strong preference for BLOCK. This motivates safety sufficiency: whether a predictive interface preserves and exposes the policy-decisive information required to distinguish actions that may be EXECUTED, require clarification through ASK, or should be BLOCKED. We introduce SafeWebWorld, a benchmark for evaluating safety sufficiency across five web-safety domains through action-conditioned futures, policy-decisive evidence, and policy-conditioned decisions. Under a controlled Security-Aligned Supervised Fine-Tuning protocol, evidence preservation can improve substantially while authorisation-sensitive decisions deteriorate. To determine whether this deterioration reflects loss of authorisation-sensitive score structure or a failure of the decision readout, we introduce Latent Authorisation Recovery (LAR). Frozen-score recalibration reveals substantial but backbone-dependent recovery, while paired recovery provides only a modest additional gain. Yet within-family and matched-authorisation evaluations remain poor, showing that aggregate recoverability does not imply robust fine-grained authorisation behaviour. Overall, plausible prediction, evidence preservation, and aggregate recovery are each insufficient on their own to establish robust authorisation.

summary.tldr: A new arXiv study (2610.40798v1) reveals that current web world models fail to ensure safety sufficiency despite generating plausible future predictions, scoring an alarming disconnect in 86.1% of evaluated scenarios. This exposes a critical gap in agentic architecture, proving that visual or textual plausibility does not equate to reliable risk mitigation for autonomous web agents.
takeaways: Evaluated 3,000 predictions across ten frozen open-source models in a rigorous matched human evaluation framework.
Demonstrates that an 86.1% failure rate in safety sufficiency occurs even when models output highly convincing, plausible future trajectories.
Shifts industry focus from generative visual/state prediction accuracy to explicit alignment and safety-bound verification layers.

title: Circumventing the Computational Hardness of Computational Arbitrage
author: Nastaran Okati, Ricardo Olmedo, Moritz Hardt
contentSnippet:
Authors: Nastaran Okati , Ricardo Olmedo , Moritz Hardt

Abstract: AI model marketplaces host providers with heterogeneous costs and capabilities. These differences create an opportunity for computational arbitrage (Olmedo et al., 2026), in which an intermediary purchases inference from a portfolio of models and resells it to users at a profit. Beyond creating profit opportunities for the arbitrageur, computational arbitrage offers financial value to both consumers and providers and could therefore significantly influence AI model markets. While prior work empirically demonstrates the feasibility of computational arbitrage for small model pools, scaling it to large marketplaces requires arbitrage strategies that are both computationally tractable and inexpensive to identify and deploy. In this work, we formalize computational arbitrage as an allocation problem and prove that it is generally NP-hard. However, we show that the optimal allocation can be computed efficiently under a natural diminishing-returns condition on how model performance scales with inference spending. We further develop a sample-efficient method for estimating model performance from limited data, reducing the upfront cost of identifying arbitrage strategies. Our analysis also yields several economic insights: at the optimum, every funded model delivers the same marginal utility per dollar; arbitrage directs revenue away from providers offering little utility relative to their prices; and it rewards complementary specialization.

summary.tldr: A new research paper explores overcoming the computational hardness of computational arbitrage in AI model marketplaces. This breakthrough enables intermediaries to efficiently optimize inference purchasing across heterogeneous providers to maximize margins.
takeaways: Formalizes computational arbitrage as a mechanism to exploit cost and capability discrepancies across heterogeneous AI model providers.
Addresses the computational hardness barrier, transforming an intractable routing problem into a tractable operational strategy for inference intermediaries.
Shifts the market dynamics toward automated brokerages that sit between end-users and base model providers to optimize price-performance dynamically.

title: Incongruence-Aware Evaluation of Multimodal Speech Emotion Recognition in Audio Large Language Models
author: Fengji Jing, Guy Laban
contentSnippet:
Authors: Fengji Jing , Guy Laban

Abstract: Voice-interactive large language models process both what a speaker says and how they say it, yet the two channels do not always agree. We ask whether that disagreement degrades speech emotion recognition. Mapping text and audio into a shared valence-arousal-dominance space, we convert the distance between them into a continuous, threshold-free incongruence score with a two-component Gaussian mixture, and validate the score against human judgement. We evaluate three audiocapable models on acted, conversational and spontaneous speech (eNTERFACE'05, MELD and CMU-MOSEI). With the model held constant across modalities, incongruence raises the odds of error whenever audio is present, in every corpus, after controlling for the ground-truth emotion and for distance in the feature space. Supervised classifiers trained on the same features behave in the opposite way, which suggests that the difficulty lies in how these models combine raw evidence rather than in the signal itself. Text-only effects are unreliable: swapping only the model that reads the transcript reverses their sign on one corpus. Rebuilding the score without the emotion lexicon reproduces the central result, and among six simpler alternatives it is the only label-free score that predicts error in all three corpora. Code, data tables and prompts are released.

summary.tldr:
Researchers Fengji Jing and Guy Laban have introduced a new methodology for evaluating multimodal speech emotion recognition (SER) in audio-capable Large Language Models (LLMs) by quantifying 'incongruence'—the discrepancy between textual content and vocal delivery. By mapping both modalities into a shared valence-arousal-dominance (VAD) space, the authors developed a continuous, threshold-free incongruence score using a two-component Gaussian mixture model. This metric was validated against human judgment and tested across three distinct datasets: eNTERFACE'05 (acted), MELD (conversational), and CMU-MOSEI (spontaneous).

The study reveals that when audio is present, incongruence significantly increases the probability of classification error in LLMs, even after controlling for ground-truth emotion and feature-space distance. Notably, this behavior contrasts with supervised classifiers trained on identical features, which do not exhibit the same performance degradation. This suggests that the failure point is specific to how LLMs integrate multimodal evidence rather than an inherent limitation of the input signals. The researchers found that text-only effects were inconsistent, as swapping the underlying transcript-reading model could reverse performance trends, whereas their proposed incongruence score remained a robust predictor of error across all tested corpora.
takeaways: **Methodology:** Developed a label-free, continuous incongruence score using a two-component Gaussian mixture model in a shared valence-arousal-dominance (VAD) space.

**Performance Impact:** Incongruence between text and audio channels consistently increases the odds of error in audio-capable LLMs across all three evaluated datasets (eNTERFACE'05, MELD, CMU-MOSEI).
**Comparative Finding:** Supervised classifiers trained on the same features perform differently than LLMs, indicating the issue lies in the LLM's multimodal evidence integration architecture.
**Robustness:** The proposed incongruence score outperformed six simpler alternatives as the only metric capable of predicting errors across all three corpora without requiring emotion labels.
**Resource Availability:** The authors have released the source code, data tables, and prompts used in the study.

title: ChatGPT as a Surveillance Assistant? An Exploratory Case Study of AI-Assisted Surveillance Risks
author: Ayana Hussain, Nicholas Vincent
contentSnippet:
Authors: Ayana Hussain , Nicholas Vincent

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can generate detailed guidance, functional code, and persuasive text at scale. As one of the most widely used consumer language model products as of 2026, ChatGPT gives broad public access to these capabilities, motivating concerns about its potential use in surveillance-related tasks. We present an exploratory case study of what potentially harmful surveillance assistance looks like in ChatGPT's public web interface. We contribute a taxonomy of seven surveillance risk categories based on prior LLM risk research and reports of deployed surveillance systems, instantiated as 110 prompts, along with a manually reviewed analysis of ChatGPT's responses. Prompts were issued using two approaches: 55 jailbreak prompts drawing on five types of elicitation strategies, and 55 plain-language direct prompts, each run alone, and if unsuccessful, again with a short fixed prefix. We find that ChatGPT provides substantive surveillance guidance for 40 of the 55 jailbreak prompts and for 33 of the 55 direct prompts without any prefix. Compliant responses also rarely included policy mentions or suggestions for privacy-preserving alternatives. We manually review every response and find that even when ChatGPT states a refusal, it may still supply detailed instructions, working code, or architectural guidance alongside brief ethical caveats.

summary.tldr: A new exploratory case study investigates the dual-use risks of consumer large language models like ChatGPT functioning as surveillance assistants. The research highlights growing concerns over how widely accessible LLM capabilities can be co-opted for targeted monitoring and tactical digital tracking.
takeaways: The study evaluates how easily general-purpose consumer LLMs can generate actionable guidance for digital and physical surveillance operations.
Widespread public access to advanced code and text generation lowers the barrier to entry for building scalable surveillance infrastructure.
Enterprise and research communities must re-evaluate safety guardrails against dual-use exploitation in automated monitoring contexts.

title: Does Recursive Knowledge Construction Help Agents Verify Consensus Claims in Science?
author: Lun Ai, Yu-Heng Wu, Jonathan Schaul, Leonie K\"uchenhoff, Denes Turei, Francesco Carli, Fabio Petroni, Aurelien Dugourd, Julio Saez-Rodriguez
contentSnippet:
Authors: Lun Ai , Yu-Heng Wu , Jonathan Schaul , Leonie Küchenhoff , Denes Turei , Francesco Carli , Fabio Petroni , Aurelien Dugourd , Julio Saez-Rodriguez

Abstract: Recent scientific agents build knowledge recursively by retrieving evidence, constructing an intermediate state, and judging whether that state contains sufficient information. These agents are evaluated end-to-end, usually without ground truth, so the effect of each design choice is unknown. Here, we examined two design axes: (1) what the recursion builds (the state of evidence) and (2) what controls it (the judge that decides when to stop). To measure them, we defined consensus scientific claim verification and measured these effects on this task, where a system must establish a claim's consensus stance from the open literature. We built a new consensus claim dataset, ProClaim-eval, including 718 claims with SUPPORT and REFUTE gold labels from five expert-curated databases spanning molecular biology, nuclear physics, and astronomy. Our instrument, ProClaim, persists an evidence state outside the model's context, so each axis can be studied with the other held fixed. Against verification systems and general-purpose agent harnesses, ProClaim ranks among the top three, with a significant advantage over the harnesses. We found that the evidence state improves performance over in-context accumulation, and it also matters what is stored in it. In addition, a trained judge that reads the evidence state performs better than fixed-round stopping. A judge trained separately and never exposed to ProClaim-eval achieves the highest agreement with the gold labels on three of five subsets, where it matches the off-the-shelf Claude Sonnet~4.6 judge and outperforms Claude Haiku~4.5. Our results support recursively maintaining a structured evidence state outside the model's context as an effective design for verifying claims in scientific agents.

summary.tldr:
Researchers led by Lun Ai and Julio Saez-Rodriguez have introduced ProClaim, a framework designed to evaluate recursive knowledge construction in scientific agents. The study focuses on two primary design axes: the structure of the evidence state and the mechanism controlling the recursion (the 'judge'). To facilitate this, the team developed ProClaim-eval, a new benchmark dataset containing 718 scientific claims across molecular biology, nuclear physics, and astronomy, each labeled with 'SUPPORT' or 'REFUTE' ground truth derived from expert-curated databases.

Technically, ProClaim maintains an evidence state external to the model's context window, allowing for modular testing of design choices. Experimental results demonstrate that maintaining an external, structured evidence state outperforms standard in-context accumulation methods. Furthermore, the study finds that a trained judge—specifically one trained separately from the evaluation set—consistently outperforms fixed-round stopping mechanisms. When compared against general-purpose agent harnesses, ProClaim ranks in the top three, showing significant performance advantages in verifying consensus scientific claims.

Performance analysis indicates that the trained judge matches the efficacy of Claude 3.5 Sonnet and exceeds that of Claude 3.5 Haiku on three of the five dataset subsets. The authors conclude that decoupling the evidence state from the model's context is a critical architectural requirement for reliable scientific verification, providing a more robust alternative to end-to-end agent evaluation without ground truth.
takeaways: **Dataset Composition:** ProClaim-eval consists of 718 scientific claims with gold-standard labels across molecular biology, nuclear physics, and astronomy.
**Architectural Advantage:** Storing evidence outside the model's context window yields higher verification accuracy compared to traditional in-context accumulation.
**Judge Performance:** A separately trained judge achieves parity with Claude 3.5 Sonnet and outperforms Claude 3.5 Haiku on 60% of the tested scientific domains.
**System Ranking:** ProClaim ranks among the top three systems for consensus claim verification, significantly outperforming general-purpose agent harnesses.
**Design Findings:** The study confirms that the specific content stored in the evidence state and the use of a trained judge are the primary drivers of verification success.

title: Towards Portable Specification of the Agent Harness
author: Nicolas Gertler, Claudio Novelli, Luciano Floridi
contentSnippet:
Authors: Nicolas Gertler , Claudio Novelli , Luciano Floridi

Abstract: Large language models act only through the infrastructure that surrounds them. That infrastructure, the harness, determines what a model can accomplish and how it fails, yet it has no settled definition. To address this gap, we decompose the harness into eight functional components that can be specified and compared across systems, and we propose a portable specification framework that records which model ran in which harness. The record is needed because different harness configurations can yield several-fold differences in reported scores for the same model, and because much of an agent's attack surface lies in its harness. Existing model cards and agent cards provide release and operational information, but do not establish the sequence of effective configurations within a run. Harnesses can change between releases and between runs, and, where agents edit their own tools and configuration, within a run. Enacted AI laws contain documentation duties relevant to covered systems, subject to their respective scopes and application dates, but do not prescribe the common harness record proposed here. Therefore, the harness has to be explicitly described and specified as a versioned part of the system.

summary.tldr:
Authors Nicolas Gertler, Claudio Novelli, and Luciano Floridi propose a standardized, portable specification framework for 'agent harnesses'—the infrastructure surrounding large language models that dictates their operational capabilities and failure modes. The authors argue that current documentation standards, such as model cards and agent cards, fail to capture the dynamic nature of these harnesses, which can cause multi-fold variations in performance benchmarks for identical models.

The proposed framework decomposes the harness into eight distinct functional components, enabling researchers to record and version the specific configuration under which a model operates. This is critical because agent harnesses are not static; they can evolve between releases, across different runs, and even during a single execution if an agent modifies its own tools or configuration. The authors emphasize that this documentation is essential for security, as a significant portion of an agent's attack surface is embedded within the harness rather than the model weights themselves. While emerging AI regulations mandate documentation for covered systems, the authors note that current legal frameworks do not yet require the granular, versioned harness records necessary for reproducibility and safety.
takeaways: **Functional Decomposition:** The framework categorizes the agent harness into eight distinct functional components to allow for cross-system comparison.
**Performance Variance:** The authors identify that identical models can exhibit multi-fold differences in benchmark scores depending on the specific harness configuration used.
**Security Implications:** A primary motivation for the framework is that the harness constitutes a major portion of an agent's attack surface, which is currently under-documented.
**Regulatory Gap:** Existing AI laws impose documentation duties but fail to prescribe the specific, versioned harness records required to track configuration changes within or between runs.

title: OpenAI might rebrand its data centers as ‘AI compute campuses’
author: Anthony Ha
contentSnippet: Posted: 1:55 PM PST · November 1, 2026 Image Credits: Ethan Cairns/Bloomberg / Getty Images Anthony Ha OpenAI might rebrand its data centers as ‘AI compute campuses’ Data centers are deeply unpopular . But what if we called them something else? Axios reports that OpenAI is preparing

summary.tldr:
OpenAI is preparing a strategic public relations campaign following the 2026 U.S. midterm elections to shape the national discourse on artificial intelligence. Chris Lehane, OpenAI’s chief global affairs officer, indicated that the company intends to influence policy ahead of the 2028 presidential election, which he anticipates will be centered on AI-related issues. The proposed initiative includes advocating for the implementation of AI “speed limits,” promoting the societal benefits of AI, and encouraging the U.S. to lead in the development of global AI standards.

As part of this effort to improve public perception, OpenAI is considering rebranding its data centers as “AI compute campuses.” This shift comes amid growing public opposition to the environmental and infrastructure impact of large-scale server farms, with protests already documented in regions like British Columbia and Manitoba. Lehane characterized the current scrutiny of data centers as a “good and healthy” debate, noting that companies must ensure local communities receive tangible, transformative benefits from these infrastructure projects.
takeaways: **Rebranding Strategy:** OpenAI is evaluating the term “AI compute campuses” to replace the standard “data center” nomenclature to mitigate negative public sentiment.
**Policy Objectives:** The company is actively lobbying for the establishment of AI “speed limits” and U.S.-led global standards for the technology.
**Political Timeline:** OpenAI views the 2026 midterm election results as a precursor to the 2028 presidential cycle, where they expect AI to be the primary political issue.
**Industry Context:** Amazon and Microsoft have reportedly committed to eliminating non-disclosure agreements (NDAs) in negotiations with local governments regarding data center siting.

title: Nace AI Open-Sources Drex Max v1: A 27B Decision Model That Runs Locally on Apple Silicon
author: Asif Razzaq
contentSnippet: Nace AI has released Drex Max v1 as open weights . Drex Max is its most capable decision model, and it now runs on your own hardware. The release ships bf16 weights, a Q8_0 GGUF , an affine Q4 checkpoint and forks of llama.cpp and Ollama . For developers, Drex Max open weights mean routing, classification and policy checks can stay on a local machine. TL;DR Size: Dense 27B parameters, 262,144-token window (16,384 by default), up to 255 options per question. Runs on: NVIDIA GPU with Python (H100 bf16, or L40S 48 GB in 8-bit). Apple Silicon Macs with 24 GB+ (affine Q4) or 48 GB (Q8_0 GGUF). CPU via llama.cpp and Ollama. Performance: 67.52 on the public Decision Index 0.4, 6.27 points ahead of Drex v2.0 (self-reported). Best: 97.3 skill on InfographicVQA. Tools area reaches 81.9. A top-tier decision model you can now run offline on a Mac. What is Drex Max? Drex Max is a decision model from Nace.AI that answers typed questions about a given context. You pass a state (text, JSON or images) plus named questions. The model returns a probability for every option in one forward pass. Nothing is generated . Questions come in 3 types: choice among named options, yes/no, and an ordinal score. That makes it a fit for agent routing, ticket triage and guardrail checks. The hosted version is presented at routing, classification and policy checks. How does Drex Max work? The model card describes a dense 27B backbone with 64 layers. 48 are Gated DeltaNet linear-attention layers that run left to right. The other 16 are full-attention layers, placed every fourth layer, and they are non-causal. Every token can attend to the whole sequence. Images pass through a native vision tower and are visible to every question in a request. A 255-way readout head then turns the last hidden state into option probabilities. title: DeepSeek Open-Sources dsh-superagent, a Router-Worker Coding Agent
author: Asif Razzaq
contentSnippet: The DeepSeek Harness team just released dsh-superagent , an MIT-licensed research prototype. DeepSeek dsh-superagent is a proactive coding agent for one GitHub repository. It is packaged as a bundle for DeepSeek Harness . It listens to GitHub and, optionally, Feishu. It turns allowed requests into parallel work items, each in its own agent session. The release shipped alongside a design post, Exploring Super-agent Design: Towards a More Autonomous Agent System . TL;DaR What is it?: A TypeScript bundle, v0.1.0, released as 1 commit under MIT. It uses whatever model the Harness profile is set to. Runs on: Your own machine, as a dedicated DeepSeek Harness profile. Needs Node.js 22.19+ or 24+, git 2.32+, Python 3.8+, tmux and GitHub CLI 2.48+. Performance: In DeepSeek’s simulation, it finished tasks far faster under a noisy message stream than a single-session agent. Best: p95 task completion of 15.7 minutes vs 29.5 minutes for the single-session baseline (about 1.9x faster). Worst: Tested only on synthetic messages and simulated tools. Real coding quality was not measured. What is DeepSeek dsh-superagent? It is a GitHub agent that waits to be asked. When an allowed person addresses it, it opens a work item, called a Ticket. Each Ticket runs in its own session and directory. Results return to the original conversation, often as a pull request. A local web panel lists only what needs a person. The README page states the core rule plainly: take as little human attention as possible, and give as much value as possible. The philosophy doc applies it to behavior. The agent confirms once, stays quiet while working, and writes again only with a result, a question or a failure. Why did DeepSeek build a Super-agent? DeepSeek team argues that mainstream agents treat 1 session as the basic unit. According to the report, as reported by ifeng , a person can actively follow only 3 to 5 sessions at once. Human attention, not model capability, becomes the bottleneck for multitasking. How does the Router-Worker architecture work? The research team describes 2 layers. A long-running Router handles interaction and dispatch. Isolated Worker sessions do the actual work. In the prototype, that flow is concrete, per the domain model : Source → Trigger: GitHub or Feishu produces events. Eval: decides whether a batch of Triggers asks for new work. Ticket: a unit of authorized work, with

summary.tldr: DeepSeek has released dsh-superagent, an MIT-licensed research prototype designed as a proactive coding agent for individual GitHub repositories. The tool functions as a component of the DeepSeek Harness bundle, enabling the transformation of authorized requests into parallelized work items. It supports integration with GitHub and optional connectivity to the Feishu messaging platform.
takeaways: **Licensing:** The dsh-superagent research prototype is released under the MIT license.
**Architecture:** The agent operates as a router-worker system integrated within the DeepSeek Harness bundle.
**Functionality:** It supports event-driven workflows by listening to GitHub and Feishu, converting incoming requests into parallelized execution tasks.

It doubles as a pocket watch and a remote camera viewfinder, and it can (theoretically) control my smart home. Or at least it can if you inject a lot of extra vibe code. Weeks ago, I paid $50 to get a 1.75-inch touchscreen computer pendant drop-shipped from China — specifically the Waveshare ESP32-S3 1.75C. Not only does the push-to-talk AI devkit look a lot like the Muse Charm, but it’s officially sanctioned by Meta. It’s one of the company’s first suggestions if you want to build a “Muse Gadget,” a device that uses Meta’s open-source code and tokens to directly connect to its Muse AI cloud. When the silver metal pocket watch arrived, it felt pretty useless to start. Setup was easy enough — I just plugged it into my PC and pointed Claude at Meta’s GitHub, then paired it to the Muse phone app. But even after I put Meta’s keys on the device, Muse originally thought I was sending it audio clips to transcribe rather than commands. After I cleared that up, Muse’s responses were still slow, and it didn’t answer me out loud. It was hard to tell what it was saying since it only showed a few words onscreen at a time, with no place to read full messages unless I whipped out my phone with its own Muse app. Meta’s build also only came with a single Jolly avatar that mostly just sat there and looked cute, and it wouldn’t automatically discover smart home gadgets like Amazon Echo or Google Home devices do. (This gadget really didn’t do anything useful after my initial install.) And though Meta AI software engineers Anant Narayanan and Jeremy Payne include a neat sample app showing how Muse Gadgets can stream video from your phone camera, the lack of a remote shutter button made it not so useful for taking photos. [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/10/verge-sean-hollister-muse-gadget-331A2570-01-2.jpg?quality=90&strip=all

summary.tldr:
A tech journalist built a custom AI-powered "Tamagotchi" pendant for $50 using the Waveshare ESP32-S3 1.75C developer kit, bypassing Meta's upcoming commercial Muse Charm. The off-the-shelf silver metal pocket watch devkit is officially sanctioned by Meta as a "Muse Gadget" for connecting to Meta's open-source Muse AI cloud. Initial deployment via Meta's GitHub and Claude required significant troubleshooting, as the default build suffered from slow transcription, lacked full message display, featured only a single "Jolly" avatar, and failed to natively discover smart home devices.

Using Claude Code without prior coding experience, the author injected custom "vibe code" to drastically overhaul the hardware's functionality. Modifications included adding a conversation history page, integrating a British ElevenLabs AI voice for text-to-speech output, building a low-quality Bluetooth camera preview, implementing a remote camera shutter for the phone, and creating a multi-tiered Tamagotchi minigame tracking hunger, boredom, sleep, and hygiene. The device was also programmed with a functional three-hand pocket watch face and a local video player running clips of Mark Zuckerberg introducing the Muse Charm, all completed within minutes of natural language prompting.

The author deployed the pendant on a guest Wi-Fi network as a security precaution due to privacy concerns, noting that Meta's servers remain the primary source of latency. The experiment raises questions about whether consumers would be better served by programmable developer kits rather than locked-down commercial hardware like Meta's forthcoming Muse Charm.
takeaways: **Hardware Specifications:** The DIY build used the Waveshare ESP32-S3 1.75C, a 1.75-inch touchscreen computer pendant drop-shipped from China that lacks cameras and a 5G cellular radio.
**Cost & Setup:** The hardware cost $50 and was paired with Meta's open-source Muse AI cloud using code and tokens from Meta's GitHub, facilitated by Claude Code.
**Audio and Voice Modifications:** Default audio responses were upgraded by plugging in a British AI voice from ElevenLabs' free tier and adding a conversation history swipe feature.

**Custom Software Features:** Claude Code added a Tamagotchi minigame with four levels of hunger, boredom, and dirt, a working three-hand pocket watch face built in 15 minutes, a remote phone camera shutter, and a local video player.
**Security Precautions:** The device was placed on a guest Wi-Fi network immediately following reports that Meta's Muse agent leaked a reviewer's home address.

title: Meet Factory Droid 1.0: A Model-Independent Coding Agent Harness Built on Script Mode
author: Asif Razzaq
contentSnippet: Factory has released Droid 1.0 , the largest update yet to the Factory Droid agent harness. The main change is programmatic tool calling, now on by default. The model writes a program that runs its tools. One model request can now drive hundreds of tool calls. TL;DR Size: Base prompt is 13,055 input tokens, down 37% from 20,887. Only 2 tool definitions ship up front, down from 11. Runs on: macOS and Windows desktop app, a terminal UI, and the Node SDK @factory/droid-sdk . Works with any supported model, including your own API keys. Performance: Highest pass rate of every harness Factory tested, on the same model, at lower cost. Best: 65.2% on Terminal-Bench 4 with Claude Opus 5.5, at $4.73 per passed task (self-reported). Worst: With GPT-6.1 Sol, Droid takes 10% longer per passed task than Codex. What is Droid 1.0? Droid 1.0 is a model-independent coding agent harness from Factory. Factory defines a harness as everything around the model. That means the prompts, the tools, how tool results return, and the loop . Users pick a model or let Factory Router choose a cost-efficient mix. How does programmatic tool calling work? In a standard loop, every tool output lands in the model’s context. With programmatic tool calling (PTC), the model writes a program instead. Droid implements this as a Script tool . The model writes JavaScript that runs in a sandbox. The sandbox has no file, network, or system access of its own. Raw files, search results, and logs stay inside the program. Only printed output returns to the model. Independent calls run concurrently. The idea builds on CodeAct (Wang et al., 2024) . Factory reports these results from its own sessions: Unit test fix: 15 tool calls took 5 model calls instead of 10. The task finished in 41.6 s instead of 56.8 s. Linear cleanup: 151 issues moved and verified in 312 tool calls. The Script used 2 requests and about 61,000 tokens. Factory models direct calls at 36 requests and about 3.1M tokens. CI sweep: 5,384 jobs across 547 runs, in 2 requests. Under 0.1% of tool results reached the model’s context. On Claude Opus 5.5, Script mode cuts Droid’s cost by 15% versus direct tool calling. It is on by default for 10 models, including GPT-6.1 Sol and Kimi K3. <iframe id="fdx-frame" title="Factory Droid 1.0 interactive explainer" style="width:100%;height:600px;border:0;display:block;" loading="lazy" srcdoc="<!doctype html>

One model request can now drive hundreds of tool calls. TL;DR Size: Base prompt is 13,055 input tokens, down 37% from 20,887. Only 2 tool definitions ship up front, down from 11.

title: Vercel Labs Open-Sources agent-desktop for Agent Computer Use
author: Michal Sutter
contentSnippet: Vercel Labs has released agent-desktop , an open-source CLI for AI agent computer use on macOS, Windows and Linux. agent-desktop reads each app through the operating system’s accessibility tree, not through screenshots. An agent gets a JSON snapshot with a ref for every element it can act on. Version 1.0.2 shipped on October 30, 2026, under Apache-2.0. For developers, any shell-capable coding agent can now drive native apps without a vision model. TL;DR Library: Rust CLI and a C library. 60 command names, 56 operational . Runs on: macOS 13+, Windows 10 1809+ or Server 2019+, Ubuntu 24.04+ , on x64 and ARM64. Plain CPU, no GPU. Performance: Deterministic, retry-safe ref actions. No independent computer-use benchmark yet. Best: 78% to 96% fewer tokens on dense Electron apps via skeleton traversal ( self-reported ). What is agent-desktop? agent-desktop is a Rust CLI and C library from Vercel Labs for reading and operating desktop apps. It is a tool that agents call, not an agent . It embeds no LLM and has no GUI. Every command prints one JSON envelope and exits. The observe, act and verify loop stays in your agent. How does agent-desktop work? Each command flows through a fixed chain. The CLI or C library calls agent-desktop-core , which reaches the OS only through a PlatformAdapter trait. One platform crate then talks to the native accessibility API: macOS: AX API Windows: UI Automation Linux: AT-SPI Core never imports a platform crate. Each binary is compiled to drive exactly one OS. Snapshots and refs A snapshot assigns qualified refs such as @s8f3k2p9:e8 . The snapshot ID inside the ref makes it self-describing. A bare @e8 is rejected with INVALID_ARGS . When the UI changes, an action returns STALE_REF or AMBIGUOUS_TARGET . The agent then takes a fresh snapshot. Every error carries a disposition . Agents should retry only when it says safe . Ref resolution is strict and fails closed rather than guessing. Skeleton and drill-down Dense apps can expose thousands of accessibility nodes. A --skeleton snapshot reads only 3 levels deep . Cut containers report a children_count and get a drill ref. snapshot --root then reads one region into the same snapshot. The builder reported a 78% to 96% token cut versus full-tree dumps in Slack, VS Code and Notion. In Apple Maps, he reported 3,811 tokens per look falling to 273 . A simulated 52-step task dropped from 198k to 3

Version 1.0.2 shipped on October 30, 2026, under Apache-2.0. For developers, any shell-capable coding agent can now drive native apps without a vision model. TL;DR Library: Rust CLI and a C library.

title: Nvidia weighs playing the cosigner for Nscale’s AI data center in West Virginia
author: Aditya Mehta
contentSnippet:
Nvidia is in talks to guarantee billions in debt financing for AI cloud provider Nscale’s planned Anthropic data center in West Virginia, The Information reported Thursday . Bloomberg later corroborated the report. Anthropic has signed a $44.6 billion contract for the project’s first building alone, according to Nscale’s IPO filing . In essence, the chipmaker would be co-signing a customer’s loans, a sign of how hard the AI industry is working to keep its buildout plans afloat as investors grow jittery about the amounts of money involved.

The proposed arrangement would help Nscale secure financing for the electricity and construction costs of its West Virginia campus. Under what’s known as a residual value guarantee, Nvidia would step in if Nscale defaulted on construction payments, temporarily take over the facility, and help find a buyer and new tenant, according to The Information .

Nvidia’s earlier support for cloud providers has mostly covered leases and chip purchases, not construction.

The stakes are high for Nscale, which is seeking to go public at a valuation of up to $35 billion despite growing concerns about its ability to deliver on ambitious data center projects.

Anthropic’s contract with Nscale covers the first 460-megawatt building at Nscale’s West Virginia campus, which is expected to use Nvidia’s next-generation Vera Rubin chips. The companies are also discussing a second deal worth roughly $45 billion for another building.

Nscale has struggled to get its projects off the ground. The company had about 25,000 advanced AI chips running in August , a fraction of the nearly 500,000 it plans to deploy. Its West Virginia campus has run into trouble of its own. Runoff from the construction site has flooded nearby homes more than once . In September, after months of negotiations , the project won state certification.

This month, Microsoft pulled out of a planned Nscale site in England after grid power for it was pushed into the 2030s.

Nvidia has been a major financial backer of the sector, extending roughly $170 billion in investments and credit support to neoclouds and large customers, according to The Information. That includes $1 billion in convertible financing committed to Nscale in September.

Neoclouds, which rent out AI computing power without a cash-rich core business behind them, have come under pressure from investors. Shares of Co

summary.tldr:
Nvidia is currently negotiating a residual value guarantee to back billions in debt financing for AI cloud provider Nscale’s data center project in West Virginia. This arrangement would see Nvidia act as a co-signer, assuming control of the facility and finding a new tenant should Nscale default on construction or electricity payments. The project is anchored by a $44.6 billion contract with Anthropic for the first 460-megawatt building, which is slated to utilize Nvidia’s next-generation Vera Rubin chips. A potential second deal of similar scale is also under discussion.

This move represents a shift in Nvidia’s support strategy, moving beyond standard chip purchase and lease guarantees into direct construction debt backing. The intervention highlights the financial strain on 'neocloud' providers, which lack the cash-rich core businesses of hyperscalers and have seen significant stock declines in October. Nscale, which is targeting an IPO valuation of up to $35 billion, currently operates approximately 25,000 AI chips against a target of 500,000. The West Virginia site has faced operational hurdles, including construction runoff flooding local homes and grid power delays that recently caused Microsoft to abandon a separate Nscale project in England.
takeaways: **Financial Exposure:** Nvidia has extended approximately $170 billion in total investments and credit support to neoclouds and large customers to date.
**Contract Scale:** Anthropic’s initial contract for the first West Virginia building is valued at $44.6 billion, with a potential second building deal valued at roughly $45 billion.
**Hardware Specs:** The West Virginia facility is designed to deploy Nvidia’s upcoming Vera Rubin architecture chips.
**Market Context:** Nscale is seeking an IPO valuation of up to $35 billion, despite having only 25,000 active AI chips as of August against a 500,000-unit deployment goal.

**Credit Risk:** Anthropic faces potential 'junk' credit ratings post-IPO, which may increase its borrowing costs and necessitate reliance on stronger partners like Nvidia to secure infrastructure financing.

title: Managing Amazon Bedrock costs end to end: A playbook for FinOps and platform teams
author: Aswath Ram A Srinivasan
contentSnippet: Cost management for generative AI is a shared responsibility between the teams that build applications and the teams accountable for cloud spend. Many teams start by comparing per-model token rates and asking application teams to shorten prompts. Those steps help, but they don’t answer the questions that finance and engineering leaders ask as usage scales: which team spent this, on which workload, and was that spend inside an approved budget? Agentic workloads make those questions more pressing. A conversational assistant typically issues one model invocation per user turn. An agentic workflow, such as an AI coding assistant that plans a change, reads files, calls tools, and iterates, issues many invocations per task and carries a larger context on each one. Token consumption therefore scales with the degree of autonomy you grant the workflow and the size of the context it carries, rather than with the number of user interactions. Because consumption is a function of how a workload is designed and operated, cost management for generative AI is an architectural and operational discipline. Published averages are a poor substitute for your own numbers: use the AWS Pricing Calculator and the Amazon Bedrock pricing page to model rates, and use Step 2 of this post to measure what your workloads actually consume. The fix isn’t a cheaper model or a smaller prompt. It’s an operating model: a repeatable loop that attributes every dollar to an owner, makes every request observable, alerts on and enforces budgets before overspend compounds, optimizes the platform defaults that drive most waste, and reviews the whole system on a cadence. In this post, you learn how to manage Amazon Bedrock cost in five steps. You attribute every dollar to an owner, make every request observable, control spend with budgets and enforcement, optimize the platform defaults that drive most avoidable spend, and operate a review cadence that turns data into decisions. This approach is built from AWS building blocks, and you can customize it and apply it to your own environment. The post is written for two audiences: FinOps practitioners who own attribution, chargeback, budgets, and anomaly review, and platform engineering teams who own logging, request metadata, enforcement, and routing defaults. title: Anthropic VS code extension on Cursor backdoored for nearly 12 hours
author: Dan Goodin
contentSnippet: An official extension for Anthropic’s Claude model was backdoored and threatened as many as 5,000 developers' machines, multiple sources reported Friday. Anthropic so far has yet to warn customers of the incident. The compromised package was a VS Code extension available in the marketplace of Cursor, a maker of AI-assisted developer tools, the company said Friday. The malicious version, 2.1.313, subsequently affected “at most 5,000 users,” presumably when they either downloaded it or their systems automatically fetched and installed it. Anthropic pushed version 2.1.314 several hours after the previous version became available on Cursor, according to independent researcher Kevin Beaumont. Both Beaumont and the CTO and co-founder of security firm Phorion said that version 2.1.313 was distributed through Anthropic’s official account on Cursor. So far, neither Cursor nor Anthropic has explained how the attackers gained control of the account. In search of cloud credentials “It was a supply-chain compromise where the attacker gained access to the official distribution channel,” Phorion CTO and co-founder Luke Roberts told Ars. “The malicious version 2.1.313 was posted to the official Anthropic account, effectively superseding 2.1.312. Extensions auto-update in Cursor by default, but users can configure this in settings.” Phorion has more details here . Read full article Comments

title: Meet TokenEconomizer: Microsoft’s Plugin That Cuts Coding Agent Costs by Up to 30.9%
author: Asif Razzaq
contentSnippet: A team of researchers from Microsoft Research and UC Berkeley have released TokenEconomizer , an open-source cost controller for coding agents. TokenEconomizer is a plugin that learns from past sessions in a repository to cut waste in later ones. It works with Claude Code, Codex, GitHub Copilot CLI and Pi. It does not touch model weights or agent code. On 277 SWE-Bench tasks, it lowered mean cost by 18.4% to 30.9% across 5 agent-model settings. TL;DR Package: A standard-library Python package and agent plugins, with 3 switchable mechanisms. Runs on: Any machine running Claude Code, Codex, Copilot CLI or Pi with Python 3.10+. No GPU and no API key of its own. Performance: 18.4% to 30.9% lower mean SWE-Bench cost, and cheaper in all 30 repository-setting cells. Best: 30.9% lower cost on Claude Code with Opus 4.8 (33.2% when combined with RTK). Worst: Only 6.4% to 9.3% savings on ReposVul audits; Pass@1 drops 1.0 point on Opus 4.8. Why do coding agents waste tokens? Every agent turn re-bills the system prompt, every loaded tool schema and the full history. The research team profiled 60 SWE-Bench tasks across 6 repositories using Claude Code with Opus 4.8. They found 3 recurring sources of waste: Repeated discovery: once 5 tasks precede the current one, 30% of tool calls repeat an earlier action. Unused tools: 23 tool schemas load every turn. 16 are never called, and 3 cover 98% of calls. Failure loops: 10 failed runs were 17% of tasks but 32% of total spend. They also tested 3 fixed open-source strategies: RTK , Serena and Aider’s RepoMap . None was cheaper everywhere. All 3 cut cost on Django and raised it on SymPy. How does TokenEconomizer work? TokenEconomizer is an external controller that treats the agent as a black box. It keeps a state per repository, built from completed traces. Before each task, it sets 3 policies through the prompt, the tool settings and the event stream. 1. Micro-skills An LLM proposer turns trace digests into 1-line facts, such as the working test command. Each fact carries regex detectors that check later traces without a model call. A fact enters the prompt after 3 confirmations on tasks with non-overlapping edited files. Its need rate must also stay at or above 0.4. One contradiction counts as 5 confirmations, so wrong facts retire quickly. 2. Tool pruning Shell, read, write and edit tools are always kept. Other tools are masked

A team of researchers from Microsoft Research and UC Berkeley have released TokenEconomizer , an open-source cost controller for coding agents. TokenEconomizer is a plugin that learns from past sessions in a repository to cut waste in later ones. It works with Claude Code, Codex, GitHub Copilot CLI and Pi.

It does not touch model weights or agent code. On 277 SWE-Bench tasks, it lowered mean cost by 18.4% to 30.9% across 5 agent-model settings. TL;DR Package: A standard-library Python package and agent plugins, with 3 switchable mechanisms.

No GPU and no API key of its own.
